anatomy.lede: A sea angel is a snail stripped down for open water: no shell, a foot reshaped into wings, and a head that hides a set of grappling tools.

hotspots.label: Head
hotspots.text: Folded inside the head are three pairs of buccal cones, which inflate in an instant to seize a sea butterfly, plus chitin hooks and a toothed radula that pull it from its shell.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: Each wing is a flap of the snail's foot, called a parapodium. The pair beat up and down, driven by a rhythm-generating circuit of nerve cells in the pedal ganglia.

hotspots.label: Second wing
hotspots.text: The sea angel swims almost constantly to hold its place in the water, and beats its wings faster when hunting or escaping danger.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The tail works as a rudder. When the body tips away from upright, it bends the opposite way to correct it.

stats.label: Survived without food in the lab

senses.lede: With simple, large nerve cells, the sea angel's senses have been traced almost cell by cell.

senses.name: Gravity sense
senses.text: Two statocysts — tiny balance organs, each holding a stone-like statolith — tell it which way is up. Receptor cells fire when they lie beneath the statolith. With the statocysts removed, a sea angel can no longer hold any steady orientation.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: A touch on the head normally triggers a defensive shutdown. But contact with its prey, the sea butterfly, sets off the whole hunting sequence instead: cones out, faster wing-beats and swimming in circles.

body.lede: Its nervous system is simple enough to study in a dish, which has made the sea angel a classic model in neuroscience.

systems.title: A built-in metronome
systems.text: Two groups of interneurons, one for the upstroke and one for the downstroke, inhibit each other in turn. The length of each inhibition largely sets how fast the wings beat.

systems.title: Serotonin for speed
systems.text: Serotonin-releasing neurons in the brain speed up swimming by recruiting extra cells into the wing circuit and strengthening the wing muscles' contractions. Stimulating the tail also speeds swimming and raises the heart rate.

genome.lede: The sea angel's DNA has been sequenced only in rough draft.

findings.title: A first rough draft
findings.text: A draft assembly of about 1.26 billion base pairs was deposited in 2023 by Iridian Genomes. It is split into more than 500,000 short pieces, so it is not yet a finished reference genome.

mind.lede: Russian and American laboratories have studied how this little snail's nervous system runs its behaviour for more than four decades.

studies.title: Hunting on a switch
studies.text: Injecting a drug that boosts the nerve messenger acetylcholine made sea angels perform the full hunting routine in response to a simple touch, or even spontaneously.

studies.title: Head up or head down
studies.text: Sea angels usually swim head up, but hold a head-down posture in warmer water and at one stage of hunting. Postural control switches off entirely during vertical migrations, defence and the 'looping' of a hunt.

studies.title: A brain steering a motor
studies.text: Researchers wired an isolated sea angel nervous system, with its statocysts, to a motor that rotated it. When the loop was closed, the neurons kept the preparation upright on their own.

studies.title: A model for changing gear
studies.text: Because it changes swimming speed to feed and to avoid predators, and its neurons can be recognised from animal to animal, the sea angel is used to study how nervous systems control speed.

survival.lede: A slow, soft-bodied snail in open water has few defences beyond speed and stamina.

tactics.title: Shut down when touched
tactics.text: A touch on the head triggers a defence reaction: the main motor systems, including swimming, the tentacles and the feeding apparatus, are inhibited for a long time.

tactics.title: Sprint away
tactics.text: Sea angels accelerate their wing-beats to escape potential predators.

tactics.title: Living on reserves
tactics.text: Stored fats carry it through long periods without prey, and lab animals survived about a year without eating.

life.lede: In the high Arctic, a sea angel takes years to grow from a speck into a winged hunter.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Sea angels are hermaphrodites, probably carrying male and female organs at the same time. They breed in spring and summer and lay eggs about 0.12 mm across.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Young larvae feed on phytoplankton, then switch to sea butterflies as they grow.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Northern animals mature at about 3 cm and can reach 7–8.5 cm, feeding almost entirely on sea butterflies.

lifespan.value: Life cycle of at least two years in Svalbard
